page_text.text:
Post‑Web Governance Theory and 
Epistemicide Diagnostics 
Abstract 
This work formalizes two foundational primitives within the SignalRupture canon. Post‑web 
governance theory maps the institutional and infrastructural conditions that emerge after the 
collapse of the legacy web’s organizing principles, where platforms replace institutions, 
algorithms replace procedures, velocity replaces deliberation, and access replaces authority. 
Epistemicide diagnostics extends de Sousa Santos’ concept of epistemicide into the digital 
and post‑web domain, establishing a structured method for identifying the destruction of 
knowledge systems through access failure, custodial collapse, provenance disruption, 
algorithmic suppression, and documentary harm. Together, these frameworks provide a 
diagnostic architecture for understanding institutional strain, archival instability, and the 
emergence of custodial burden in high‑velocity governance environments. 
Keywords 
post‑web governance; epistemicide; diagnostics; archival integrity; access failure; custodial 
collapse; provenance disruption; algorithmic suppression; documentary heritage; institutional 
strain; SignalRupture 
1. Post‑Web Governance Theory 
Post‑web governance theory describes the institutional and epistemic conditions that arise after 
the collapse of the legacy web’s organizing principles. Governance no longer resides in stable 
institutions but in dynamic, adversarial, and rapidly mutating digital infrastructures. Platforms 
function as de facto institutions; algorithms act as procedures; velocity replaces deliberation; 
and access becomes the primary vector of authority. 
In this environment, archives destabilize, provenance becomes contested, visibility is 
weaponized, and custodial responsibility becomes unclear. Post‑web governance theory 
provides the conceptual tools to diagnose rupture, erosion, drift, and containment in systems 
that can no longer metabolize informational strain. 
2. Epistemicide Diagnostics

Epistemicide diagnostics is the analytical method for identifying and measuring the destruction 
of knowledge systems in post‑web environments. Extending de Sousa Santos’ concept of 
epistemicide, this framework examines five primary indicators: 
●​ Access Failure — communities cannot reach their own knowledge due to infrastructural 
decay or permissions breakdown. 
●​ Custodial Collapse — institutions fail to maintain archival integrity or continuity of care. 
●​ Provenance Disruption — authorship, lineage, or identity is severed or obscured. 
●​ Algorithmic Suppression — digital systems bury, distort, or de‑prioritize knowledge. 
●​ Documentary Harm — archives become adversarial to the people they represent. 
Epistemicide diagnostics reframes epistemicide as a governance failure rather than an isolated 
event, offering a structured methodology for assessing when institutions can no longer protect 
the epistemic rights of the communities they serve. 
3. Interlocking Frameworks 
Post‑web governance theory describes the environment in which institutions fail. Epistemicide 
diagnostics describes the consequences of that failure. Together, they form the analytical 
backbone for understanding institutional strain, archival instability, whistleblower trajectories, 
custodial burden, and the need for safe‑harbor governance architectures. 
4. Canonical Paragraph 
Post‑web governance theory and epistemicide diagnostics establish the environmental and 
diagnostic foundations for analyzing institutional collapse in the post‑web era. Post‑web 
governance theory maps the infrastructural conditions that destabilize archives, erode custodial 
responsibility, and produce adversarial visibility regimes. Epistemicide diagnostics provides a 
structured method for identifying the destruction of knowledge systems through access failure, 
custodial collapse, provenance disruption, algorithmic suppression, and documentary harm. 
Together, these frameworks reveal when institutions can no longer protect the epistemic rights 
of the communities they serve and when individuals are forced to become the last custodians of 
truth.
